assessment.nobel_worthiness: Opening a genuinely new observational window: a cubic-kilometre detector built in Antarctic ice that detected high-energy astrophysical neutrinos. This is detector-driven discovery of the kind I value, and it launched neutrino astronomy as a field.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led the cubic-kilometre concept and IceCube; Karle and Spiering are credited as central to construction, analysis and the discovery. A three-person split is plausible, but I cannot independently verify the relative weight of the many senior collaboration figures, and some other leaders of IceCube or its predecessor AMANDA could be argued for.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux was found in 2013 and has been confirmed by multiple independent analyses. The blazar TXS 0506+056 association (2018) and Galactic-plane neutrinos (2023) have followed, so the result is mature and timely.
uncertainties: The sources of the bulk of the diffuse flux are still unresolved, though the discovery itself is not in doubt.
Credit among IceCube and AMANDA founders and collaboration leaders is a judgment call.
Whether KM3NeT or Baikal results should figure in the citation is unclear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Experimental discovery of the Higgs boson at the LHC in 2012 completed the Standard Model. It is a major, clear and lasting result, and the detectors and trigger and analysis systems behind it are extraordinary instrumentation achievements. The 2013 prize recognised the theory; the experimental side has not been recognised.
assessment.attribution: The ATLAS and CMS experiments each involved thousands of people. Experiment leadership (spokespersons and the founding proposers) is the natural, if imperfect, basis for a prize. Four names are credited and at most three can be chosen, so someone from one of the experiments is left out. I choose Gianotti and Jenni from ATLAS and Virdee from CMS, but this leaves Della Negra with a comparable claim and could be seen as unbalanced.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by two experiments and by years of measurements of couplings. Fully mature; if anything, late.
uncertainties: Allocation of credit among the two collaborations and between spokespersons and detector founders is contested.
The Nobel statutes' three-person limit sits awkwardly with collaborations of this size.
The 2013 prize may weigh against a further Higgs-related award in the committee's view.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, with its magic-wavelength trapping idea and realisation, brought fractional uncertainties to the 10^-18 level. It is now redefining timekeeping and enabling tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy. This is a major measurement technology advance.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength optical lattice concept and demonstrated the first clock; Ye led the realisation of the highest-performance strontium lattice clocks. The pairing is clean, though others (for example Hall and Hänsch were already honoured in 2005 for combs, and ion-clock work was honoured in 2012) form context rather than competition.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmation across many laboratories; international comparisons. A redefinition of the SI second is being prepared. Timely and stable.
uncertainties: Field is outside my own expertise, and I rely on atomic physics colleagues for the credit attribution.
Overlap with earlier prizes (2005 comb, 2012 quantum control) could be seen as incremental by some members.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ground-based very-high-energy gamma-ray astronomy through imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes opened the TeV sky, revealing hundreds of sources including supernova remnants, pulsar wind nebulae, and active galaxies. It is a field close to my own and a clear example of an instrument-led window on the universe.
assessment.attribution: Aharonian led the theory and the HEGRA and H.E.S.S. programmes; Hofmann led H.E.S.S. as spokesperson and builder. The imaging Cherenkov technique itself owes much to Weekes and the Whipple group (the Crab detection in 1989), who are not among the credited names. This is a significant unresolved attribution problem for a fair prize citation.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent instruments (H.E.S.S., MAGIC, VERITAS) have confirmed the results over two decades; CTAO is under construction. The field is mature.
uncertainties: The Whipple pioneers (Weekes and colleagues) are absent from the credited names, so a prize limited to the credited names may be seen as incomplete.
Whether the discovery is the technique or the astrophysical results is not obvious.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The first horizon-scale images of M87* (2019) and Sgr A* (2022) are direct visual evidence of black-hole shadows. The very long baseline interferometry achievement at 1.3 mm is a great instrumentation and calibration feat, and the images are of broad public and scientific impact.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed the shadow imaging concept; Doeleman built and led the EHT collaboration; Zensus led the European VLBI side and the MPIfR contribution. Allocation relative to the 300-strong collaboration and to earlier VLBI pioneers is unresolved, and the credited set may not be fair.
assessment.maturity: Two independent targets and several epochs, consistent with general relativity within limited precision. Still a young result, and images depend on reconstruction methods, so more time for polarisation and dynamics results would strengthen it.
uncertainties: Image reconstruction systematics and interpretation of the ring remain debated in places.
Credit allocation within a very large collaboration is delicate.
The 2020 prize already recognised black-hole physics, so overlap should be weighed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Silicon microstrip and pixel detectors transformed vertex and tracking measurements at every collider and in space, from heavy-flavour physics to the Higgs discovery. The Nobel Prize in Physics has recognised detector inventions before (Charpak 1992), and this is a foundational enabling technology that I know well from my own field.
assessment.attribution: Parker (microstrip and 3D concepts), Heijne and Weilhammer (the early CERN silicon work, NA11 and pixel developments) are credible, but the invention history is diffuse: Kemmer's planar process for silicon detectors and Hyams and others from the early 1980s are not listed here. I cannot independently settle the priority.
assessment.maturity: The technology is ubiquitous and has been validated for four decades. It is fully mature, but there is a risk that the community sees the work as engineering rather than a discovery.
uncertainties: Priority and attribution among early silicon detector developers is contested and I cannot resolve it here.
Whether the committee regards an enabling technology as sufficiently fundamental physics is open.
The wider development, including CMOS sensors and readout chips, spreads credit widely.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond led to a robust room-temperature quantum sensor with applications from nanoscale magnetometry to biological sensing. Quantum sensors are an area where basic work leads to practical devices.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko did the 1997 single-centre optical detection and the early coherent control; Lukin developed the sensing and many-body applications. Other groups (Awschalom, Hanson, Yacoby, Walsworth) also made decisive contributions, so a three-name selection leaves substantial parts out.
assessment.maturity: Replicated widely; commercial devices exist. Reliable and broadly confirmed. The topic is outside my direct expertise, so I defer to colleagues in atomic and quantum physics.
uncertainties: Credit is spread over several leading groups and the three-name set is a contestable choice.
The relative importance of sensing versus quantum-information uses is not obvious.
Recent prizes in quantum technology may reduce room for an additional award in that area.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background from pulsar timing arrays (2023) opens a new gravitational-wave band by exploiting millisecond pulsars as a galaxy-sized detector. It is a fascinating new window with clear instrumentation and analysis foundations.
assessment.attribution: The signal is the product of NANOGrav, EPTA/InPTA, PPTA and CPTA, each with large teams, and long-standing leadership. Kramer (EPTA), Hobbs (PPTA) and Siemens (NANOGrav) represent the three main collaborations, but the credited list also includes McLaughlin. The choice of three is arbitrary, and a fair assignment looks difficult.
assessment.maturity: Evidence is around 3-4 sigma for Hellings-Downs correlations and not yet a definitive detection. The origin (supermassive black hole binaries versus new physics) is not settled. Recognition now would be premature.
uncertainties: The significance is below the conventional discovery threshold in most analyses.
The source of the background is not established.
Credit is spread across four collaborations and a clean three-person prize is hard.
